articles.title: The Man Who Came Back to the Fire
articles.dek: Peter once warmed his hands by a charcoal fire and denied he knew Jesus. Thirty years later, his last letter shows what God does with a torn and failed life.
articles.quote: The God who mends torn nets still sends them back into the water.
articles.body:
On a cold October night in 1986, at Shea Stadium in New York, a slow ground ball rolled toward Bill Buckner, the veteran first baseman of the Boston Red Sox. His team was one game away from its first World Series title since 1918, and the score in the tenth inning was already tied. The ball skipped low, slipped between his legs and rolled into right field as the winning run crossed home plate. Boston lost that game and then lost the series two nights later, and for almost twenty years one tired man with bad ankles carried the blame for an entire city's heartbreak.

Fans booed him for seasons afterward. The clip played on television every October, and his family heard cruel things from strangers. In time Buckner moved his family across the country to Idaho, far from the noise. Then the Red Sox finally won the World Series in 2004 and again in 2007, and on April 8, 2008, the team invited him back to Fenway Park to throw the ceremonial first pitch at the home opener. When he walked in from left field, the whole ballpark rose to its feet and kept applauding, minute after minute, until the old first baseman had to wipe his eyes before he could throw.

Filipinos feel this story in the body. We know hiya, the heavy shame of failing in front of people who matter to us, and we know the titos who bring up our worst moment at every reunion. Scripture tells a story like Fenway's, except the welcome comes first from God, and the man who receives it spends the rest of his life passing it on.

Picture a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard in Jerusalem, sometime after midnight. Simon Peter, who had sworn only hours earlier that he would die before deserting Jesus, stands warming his hands among servants and guards. A servant girl studies his face and says he was with the prisoner. He denies it, then denies it again, and the third time he swears an oath, and somewhere a rooster crows. Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter, and Peter went outside and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

John is the only Gospel writer who tells us what kind of fire it was. He uses the Greek word anthrakia, a fire of charcoal, in John 18:18, and he uses it only once more. Weeks after the resurrection, Peter and a few friends had gone back to fishing on the Sea of Galilee, caught nothing all night, and at dawn saw a figure on the shore. When they came in, they found Jesus cooking breakfast over "a fire of burning coals" (John 21:9). Beside that second charcoal fire, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him, one question for each denial, and each time he gave him work to do, ending with "Feed my sheep" (John 21:15–17).

Now move forward about thirty years. Peter is an old man, most likely in Rome, which he calls "Babylon" in a kind of early Christian code (1 Peter 5:13). He is writing to scattered believers in what is now Turkey who are being slandered and pushed to the margins for their faith, and in his closing chapter he speaks directly to their church leaders.

"To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed: Be shepherds of God's flock that is under your care." (1 Peter 5:1–2)

Every phrase in that sentence carries the memory of a fire. Peter calls himself "a witness of Christ's sufferings," and the honest truth is that he watched part of those sufferings from a courtyard while pretending he had never met the Man. He could have quietly left that out. Instead he signs his appeal with the very credential that once shamed him, and the instruction he hands on, "Be shepherds," is the same one Jesus gave him on the beach. The apostle who had been welcomed home now stands at the gate, welcoming others in.

The most beautiful echo comes a few verses later: "And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast" (1 Peter 5:10). The Greek verb translated "restore" is katartizō, and it was a fisherman's word. Mark uses it when Jesus first finds James and John in a boat "preparing their nets" (Mark 1:19), meaning they were repairing the torn places so the nets could be cast again. Peter had been fishing beside those very boats that day. One way to read his promise is as a quiet autobiography: God took a man torn open by failure, mended him knot by knot, and sent him back into the water.

The chapter is full of small memories like this. When Peter tells everyone to "clothe yourselves with humility" (1 Peter 5:5), the verb enkombōsasthe means to tie something on with a knot, the way a servant tied on a work apron. It is hard to read that without remembering the night Jesus wrapped a towel around his waist and knelt to wash Peter's protesting feet (John 13:4–8). When he warns that the devil "prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour" (1 Peter 5:8), he writes as the man who fell asleep in Gethsemane after Jesus asked him to keep watch (Mark 14:37). Peter knows exactly where the weak places are, because he has been mended in each of them.

In his final greetings he mentions "my son Mark" (1 Peter 5:13). This is almost certainly John Mark, the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through their first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), so that Paul later refused to take him again (Acts 15:37–39). Early church tradition remembers Mark as Peter's interpreter and the writer of the Gospel that bears his name. The deserter had found a spiritual father who knew all about deserting, and who had learned from Jesus what to do with someone who comes back. Years later even Paul would write that Mark was "helpful to me in my ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11).

This is where the passage meets us. Most of us carry a moment like that ground ball or that courtyard: a word we cannot take back, a season when we ran, a failure people still mention. Shame urges us to stay in Idaho, far from anyone who remembers, yet Peter's letter suggests that the place where God mended you may become the place where you are most useful to someone else. The parent who once lost their temper often becomes the gentlest listener for a young mother at the end of her rope, and the friend who has walked out of addiction can sit with someone at three in the morning and say, with complete honesty, "I know."

You might begin today by naming, privately before God, the failure you are still most ashamed of, and asking him the question that hangs over that second fire: what would you have me do with this? Then look around for one Mark in your life, someone who has recently stumbled and is waiting to see whether anyone will still make room for them. A message or an invitation to merienda, with a sincere "Kumusta ka na talaga?", may be the first knot in their mending.

Bill Buckner threw his pitch that April afternoon while a crowd that once booed him kept cheering. Peter received an even greater welcome on a quiet beach, with only a handful of friends watching and the smell of charcoal in the air. The God who mends torn nets still sends them back into the water. Whatever tore you, the God of all grace "will himself restore you" (1 Peter 5:10), and then he will hand you someone to shepherd.

articles.title: Measured Before It Was Built
articles.dek: Fourteen years after Jerusalem burned, God sent an angel with a measuring rod to a temple that did not exist yet. Love tends to work this way.
articles.quote: God measures what he means to keep, and he takes the measurements long before we can see anything standing.
articles.body:
Every May, in towns from Ilocos to Davao, a small ritual plays out in the front room of the neighborhood mananahi. A mother brings in her child, still sun-browned from summer, to be measured for the new school uniform. The dressmaker runs a yellow tape across the child's shoulders and down from hip to knee, then writes the numbers in pencil in a worn notebook. Before they leave, the mother says the line almost every Filipino child has heard over their own head: "Lakihan mo nang kaunti, Ate, para hindi agad masikipan." Make it a little bigger, so it still fits by December.

That exchange is quietly tender. No cloth has been cut and the school year has not started, yet two women are already planning for a child who will be taller in six months. Without saying so, they assume a future in which this boy or girl is still here, still growing, still walking to class every morning. A measurement taken in love works like a promise, because it tells the child that someone is expecting them.

I thought of that front room while reading Ezekiel 40, a chapter many readers skim because it seems to be all numbers. Gates, thresholds, alcoves, and porches, each with its length and width given in cubits, go on for verse after verse. The numbers, though, are the message, and they make sense once you know who received them and when.

Ezekiel was a priest, "the son of Buzi" (Ezekiel 1:3), taken to Babylon in 597 BC along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. Eleven years later the Babylonian army broke through the walls of Jerusalem and burned Solomon's temple. Chapter 40 opens with a careful date: "In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month, in the fourteenth year after the fall of the city" (Ezekiel 40:1). That puts us around 573 BC. For fourteen years God's people had lived without the building that told them God lived among them, and a whole generation of children had grown up knowing the temple only as a story their grandparents told through tears.

The date also carries a personal sadness. Ezekiel's book begins "in my thirtieth year" (Ezekiel 1:1), and many scholars take that to be his age, the year a priest would normally begin serving. If so, he was now about fifty, the age when Levites retired from temple duty (Numbers 8:25). He had trained his whole life for a sanctuary and never served in it for a single day. His career came and went in a foreign land, beside a canal in Babylon.

"On that very day," the verse continues, "the hand of the LORD was on me and he took me there" (Ezekiel 40:1). In a vision God set him "on a very high mountain, on whose south side were some buildings that looked like a city" (40:2). At the gateway stood a figure "whose appearance was like bronze," holding "a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand" (40:3). Then this man began to walk, and everywhere he went he measured. He measured the east gate and its steps, the threshold and the guard alcoves, and the thickness of the walls. He crossed the outer court, measured the north and south gates, went up into the inner court, and measured the tables where offerings would be prepared and the rooms for the singers and the priests. The chapter closes at the center of it all: "Then he measured the court: It was square, a hundred cubits long and a hundred cubits wide. And the altar was in front of the temple" (40:47).

Before any of the measuring began, the man stopped and spoke to the old priest.

"Son of man, look carefully and listen closely and pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here. Tell the people of Israel everything you see." (Ezekiel 40:4)

The Hebrew of that verse is wonderfully physical. Read literally, it says "see with your eyes, hear with your ears, and set your heart." Ezekiel was being asked for more than a glance. God wanted his full attention, the kind a dressmaker gives to a child standing very still with arms held out.

The tool itself tells a story too. The man's measuring rod is a qaneh, the Hebrew word for a reed, "six long cubits" (40:5), or roughly three meters. It is a distant ancestor of our word "canon," the standard by which something is measured. In Scripture, measuring is what God does with something he intends to claim and protect. Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line set out to measure Jerusalem, and the promise follows that God himself will be "a wall of fire around it" (Zechariah 2:1–5). John is handed a reed and told to "measure the temple of God" (Revelation 11:1), and at the very end of the Bible an angel measures the new Jerusalem with "a measuring rod of gold" (Revelation 21:15). From one end of the Bible to the other, when heaven takes out a measuring rod, it means that God has plans for this place and intends to stay.

Some scholars see another layer in that opening date. The "tenth of the month" at the turning of the year recalls the day the trumpet was sounded to begin the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and land went back to its families (Leviticus 25:9–10). Jubilee came every fiftieth year, and the twenty-fifth year of exile falls exactly halfway there. Read this way, the timing itself suggests that the exiles were halfway home. It also matters that the measuring starts at the east gate, the direction in which Ezekiel had watched God's glory leave the city years before (Ezekiel 11:23). Three chapters later, that same glory comes back "from the east" (43:2). The angel was measuring a home for God's own return.

The most human part of the story comes at the end of the verse: "Tell the people of Israel everything you see." The vision was given to a tired man so he could hand it on to tired neighbors. Hope that God measures out to us is rarely meant for us alone. It is meant to be carried to the person beside us, who is still waiting for their walls to go back up.

Most of us know someone living in their own fourteenth year after the fall. It may be a parent who has worked abroad for a decade and wonders whether home will still feel like home, or a friend who has been rebuilding slowly since a marriage ended. It may be a young cousin who failed the board exam and has stopped talking about the future. When people are in ruins, the loving thing to do is often what that bronze figure did: slow down and pay attention to the details. Ask about the specific thing they are afraid of, remember the name of the boss who has been difficult, and make a plan with them for next month as if you fully expect them to be there. Like the mother at the mananahi, leave a little room for them to grow.

The same truth is for you. You may feel like Ezekiel at fifty, sure that the season you trained for has passed and that whatever was meant to be built in your life burned down a long time ago. Ezekiel 40 says that on the very day the old priest felt furthest from his calling, God brought him to the high mountain and showed him what was coming, one careful cubit at a time. God measures what he means to keep, and he takes the measurements long before we can see anything standing.

Today, pick one person whose life feels unfinished and give them that kind of attention. Ask, listen, and plan something with them. Then believe the same thing about yourself: the tape is already around your shoulders, and the One holding it is expecting you.

articles.title: Ringed by Mountains
articles.dek: Jerusalem was lower than the hills around it, and the pilgrims who sang Psalm 125 knew it. A village in the French highlands helps show where a steady life gets its strength.
articles.quote: The steadiest people are the ones who know they are surrounded.
articles.body:
In the winter of 1940, a frightened woman knocked on a door in a small village high on a plateau in south-central France. She was a German Jew running from the Nazis. She had made her way through the cold to Le Chambon-sur-Lignon because she had heard that people there might help. The woman who opened the door was Magda Trocmé, wife of the village's Protestant pastor. Years later, people asked Magda why she did what she did next, and the question seemed to puzzle her. All she remembered was telling the stranger, "Naturally, come in, and come in."

That door turned out to be the first of many. Over the next four years, the farmers, shopkeepers and schoolteachers of the Vivarais-Lignon plateau hid thousands of refugees, many of them Jewish children, in their homes, boarding schools and barns. In June 1940, just after France signed its armistice with Germany, André Trocmé and his fellow pastor Édouard Theis had preached that Christians must resist the violence brought against their consciences with "the weapons of the Spirit." Their congregation believed them. When officials came asking for a list of the Jews in the village, Trocmé is remembered to have answered that he did not know what a Jew was, only human beings. In 1990, Israel's Yad Vashem honored the whole community as Righteous Among the Nations.

What moves me most is how ordinary the shelter was. A refugee child on that plateau was held by a whole circle of people: the baker who kept quiet, the neighbor who sent word that a raid was coming, the farm family who always kept a spare bed made up. Her safety came from being surrounded. That picture is close to the heart of one of the gentlest psalms in the Bible.

Psalm 125 is one of fifteen short songs, Psalms 120 to 134, that carry the title "A song of ascents." Most scholars think pilgrims sang them on the way up to Jerusalem for the great yearly festivals. Picture a family from Galilee, several days into the trip, with sore feet and dust on their clothes, children asking how much farther. The last part of the road climbs steeply through the Judean hills. Then they come over a ridge and there is the city, gold in the afternoon light, with hills on every side. That is the moment this song was written for.

"Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be shaken but endures forever. As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:1–2)

Any pilgrim who walked that road knew a simple fact about the land: Mount Zion is a modest hill. Jerusalem sits on ridges that are lower than several of the hills around it. The Mount of Olives, just across the Kidron Valley to the east, rises well above the old city, and travelers had to climb past higher ground before they reached the Temple. The psalmist could have praised Zion for towering over everything. He gave the pilgrims two pictures side by side instead: the mountain that holds firm, and the hills standing guard around it.

One way to read this is that a person who trusts God stands firm because of what stands around them. Many of us feel more like a small hill than a great peak. We are tired, we are unsure, and we do not feel especially strong. The psalm makes room for exactly that kind of person. God's people are steady the way Jerusalem was steady, held in place by Someone greater who has drawn a ring around them.

The Hebrew words fill this out. "Cannot be shaken" translates lo yimmot, from a verb, mot, that describes something tottering or slipping, like a foot on loose stones. David used the same word in Psalm 16:8: "Because he is at my right hand, I will not be shaken." The word behind "surround" is sabib, which means "all around" or "on every side." In this picture God leads from the front and also guards the back and both flanks. Scripture returns to the image often. "The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and he delivers them," says Psalm 34:7. When Elisha's servant woke to find an enemy army around their town, Elisha prayed that his eyes would be opened, and the young man saw "the hills full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha" (2 Kings 6:17). The danger was real, and a greater ring stood around it.

The next verse holds a tenderness that is easy to pass over. "The scepter of the wicked will not remain over the land allotted to the righteous, for then the righteous might use their hands to do evil" (Psalm 125:3). Many scholars believe this song comes from a time when God's people lived under foreign rule. The psalmist admits something honest here: if pressure goes on long enough, even good people can start to bend. They may cut corners, grow bitter, or give up on doing right. God knows this about us, and so he sets a limit on how long the scepter of the wicked may stay. Paul says the same thing centuries later: "And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The God who surrounds you also knows where your breaking point is, and he keeps watch over it.

On the plateau in France, the occupation lasted four long years. Pastor Trocmé was arrested in 1943 and held in an internment camp for several weeks. Families lived with the fear of a knock in the night. But the scepter did not stay, and in 1944 the region was set free. The children hidden in those farmhouses grew up, and many of them lived to tell their own grandchildren about the people who had stood around them.

Filipinos understand this psalm better than they might realize. The Sierra Madre runs along the eastern edge of Luzon, and when typhoons come in from the Pacific, those mountains often break their strength before they reach the lowlands. Millions of people in Central Luzon and Metro Manila go through storm season without thinking much about the range to the east, yet it guards them year after year. This is how the psalm describes the life of a person who trusts God. Much of your protection is invisible, and most days you never see it. The ring is there all the same.

You might carry this into today in two simple ways. Tonight, before you sleep, pray Psalm 125:2 with your own name in it: "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds me, both now and forevermore," and then name one burden you can rest inside that circle. Then ask God to show you one person who needs a hill standing beside them right now, perhaps a relative far from home, a coworker going through a hard season, or a friend who has gone quiet, and send that person a message or knock on their door before the week is over. Magda Trocmé never thought of herself as brave. She simply opened the door, and her neighbors closed ranks around the people who came in.

The psalm ends with a short blessing: "Peace be on Israel" (Psalm 125:5). It is a fitting word for tired travelers who have just reached the top of the road. The steadiest people are the ones who know they are surrounded. Whatever slope you are climbing this weekend, the hills around you are higher than the trouble ahead of you, and the Lord who set them there is standing on every side of you, today and for every day still to come.

articles.title: The Soft Word That Breaks Bone
articles.dek: A young Benjamin Franklin won over a hostile rival by borrowing a book. Solomon's court proverb shows why gentle patience reaches hearts that force cannot, and it's the same way God reached ours.
articles.quote: Gentleness is the strength that outlasts a hard heart, because it is the very way God won yours.
articles.illustration: Benjamin Franklin borrows a rival's book
articles.body:
In 1737, a young Philadelphia printer named Benjamin Franklin had a problem with a powerful man. Franklin had recently been chosen clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, and when his reappointment came up, a new member, wealthy and well educated, stood and gave a long speech against him. Franklin could see that this man's influence in the colony would only grow. He could have answered with flattery, or he could have fought back in kind. He chose something so small that it hardly seems worth writing down.

Franklin had heard that the gentleman owned a rare and curious book. He wrote him a short, courteous note asking if he might borrow it for a few days. The man sent it at once. About a week later Franklin returned it with a second note thanking him warmly for the favor. Years afterward, in his Autobiography, Franklin described what followed: "When we next met in the House, he spoke to me (which he had never done before), and with great civility; and he ever after manifested a great readiness to serve me on all occasions, so that we became great friends, and our friendship continued to his death."

Franklin connected the episode to an old saying he had learned: "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged." Psychologists still call this the Ben Franklin effect. The same book records a second habit that may matter even more. As a young man Franklin loved to win arguments and enjoyed cornering people. Slowly he trained himself to drop words like "certainly" and "undoubtedly," and to say instead, "I conceive" or "it so appears to me at present." People listened to him more readily, and when he turned out to be wrong, he lost fewer friends. The man who would later help persuade France to support a struggling young nation had learned his craft by speaking softly.

Nearly three thousand years before Franklin, a collection of court sayings in the Bible had already put this lesson into a single line. Proverbs 25 opens with a note from its editors: "These are more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). Hezekiah reigned more than two centuries after Solomon, and his scribes gathered these sayings for people who lived close to power, the officials and messengers who had to stand before a king and speak well.

That setting explains why verses 11 to 15 read like a handbook for the royal court. "Like apples of gold in settings of silver is a ruling rightly given" (Proverbs 25:11). "Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is the rebuke of a wise judge to a listening ear" (Proverbs 25:12). A reliable messenger is "like a snow-cooled drink at harvest time" (Proverbs 25:13), while the person who brags about gifts he never gives is "like clouds and wind without rain" (Proverbs 25:14). Then the section closes with its sharpest image.

"Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone." (Proverbs 25:15)

Imagine a royal counselor who needs to change a king's mind. The king holds the power of life and death, so he cannot be shouted down, and he cannot be forced. The proverb names two things that can succeed where pressure would fail. The first is patience. The Hebrew phrase is 'orek appayim, which literally means "length of nostrils." In Hebrew idiom, anger shows itself in hot breath flaring through the nose, so a person with a "long nose" is someone whose temper takes a very long time to heat up. The second is a gentle tongue, lashon rakkah. The word rak means soft or tender, and it is the same word Jacob uses about his small children when he tells Esau, "My lord knows that the children are tender" (Genesis 33:13).

Then comes the surprise. This soft, tender tongue "can break a bone." The word for bone, gerem, refers to the hardest part of the body, the frame that holds a person upright. The proverb pictures a stubborn will as bone, and it claims that softness can reach a place hammers cannot. One way to understand this is that hardness meeting hardness only produces more hardness, since every sharp word gives the other person something to push against. A gentle word gives them nothing to resist, so their defenses have nowhere to land. Proverbs says the same thing elsewhere: "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1).

The phrase 'orek appayim carries an even deeper meaning. Before it ever described a wise courtier, it described God. When the Lord passed in front of Moses on Sinai, He announced His own name: "The LORD, the LORD, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). "Slow to anger" is the same long-nosed patience found in Proverbs 25:15. The quality this proverb asks of us is, first of all, the character of the One who made us.

That is how the gospel, the good news about Jesus, actually reached us. Every human heart has its own hard bone, a proud will that would rather run its own life. God could have broken it by force. He chose patience and tenderness instead. Paul asks whether we show contempt for the riches of God's kindness, "not realizing that God's kindness is intended to lead you to repentance" (Romans 2:4). Peter writes that the Lord "is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). And Jesus describes Himself in these words: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). At the cross, the gentlest man who ever lived opened His arms to His enemies, and hearts that had resisted God for a lifetime were finally won. Gentleness is the strength that outlasts a hard heart, because it is the very way God won yours.

This changes how we handle our own hard conversations. Most of us have a "ruler" whose mind we would love to change: a manager who dismisses our ideas, a parent who is set in their ways, a teenager who has stopped listening, or a spouse who no longer brings up a certain subject. Filipino culture already knows how valuable a soft approach can be. We speak of malumanay speech and of choosing the right tiyempo, the right moment. Yet when we feel hurt, our noses tend to get short very quickly. We push harder, raise our voices, and send the long message at midnight, and then we wonder why the bone only gets harder.

Proverbs 25 suggests a different path. Gentleness here still speaks the truth, because the counselor in this verse fully intends to persuade the king. What changes is the pace and the tone. You can let a hard conversation wait one more day so that your anger has time to cool. You can use Franklin's humble phrases, such as "it seems to me" or "I might be wrong, but," which leave the other person room to agree without losing face. You might even try his strangest tactic and ask the difficult person for a small favor, or quietly do one for them, giving goodwill a door to walk through. Above all, you can pray before you speak, asking the Lord who was patient with you to lend you some of His patience.

Results may take time, and that is exactly what the word patience promises. Franklin's rival did not change overnight, and the king in Proverbs is persuaded "through patience," which means over a long stretch of time. So think of one hard heart in your life today. Before the day ends, send that person one soft word, maybe a thank-you, a question, or a simple kindness. Then trust the God who softened your own heart to keep working on theirs, gently and patiently, just as He did with you.
